title: Is This Brilliant chat?
reviewNotes: Captions and native complete diagrams reviewed. Native38 confirms the complete seventeen-piece final board after Ne5: White Kg2/Ra1/Nb1/Bf2/a2/b2/c3/g3/h2 against Kg8/Rd1/Ne5/a7/b7/e2/g7/h7, White to move. Independent h3 allows all four legal e1 promotions. Only e1=N+ gives check against Kg2; Q/R/B promotion does not. In every selected comparison Bxe1/Rxe1 legally exchanges the promoted piece and bishop into the SAME complete fifteen-piece ending. These are independently supplied alternatives, not recovered source moves or a certified forced sequence. The knight check does not prevent the bishop from capturing on e1. The full outcomes for other White moves, every promotion alternative and the larger rook/knight/pawn conversion remain pending. The original friendly-game ending was unrecorded/unremembered; no continuation is invented as actual play. All prior drafts, source images/captions and review history remain preserved.
transcript: What defines a brilliant move? Is it the fact that it's a sacrifice? Is it the follow-up of that move? Well, allow me to show you this game that I played against my friend Rachel, and I want you to decide whether a move I played is brilliant or not. This was a blitz friendly game. In this position, Rachel plays knight to d4, now attacking the bishop and the knight at the same time, except that both of these pieces are pinned by one of the white pieces, but I had something prepared. Here I simply castled and sacrificed one of my pawns because at the end of this line, there is a beautiful idea starting with bishop takes f2 check. The idea is that the bishop can, of course, not be taken because after knight to e4, this is a double check on the king, and if the king goes back, now queen b6 forces the king to a corner, and once the king goes to the corner, we can fork the king and queen and win the game. But since Rachel is a very strong player, she saw all of these threats and played king to h1. Unfortunately, though, after knight to e4, I am still creating way too many threats around the king, and so she decided to give up an exchange by taking the knight, and after I take back with the pawn, she can trade the queens, and now at least the attack is over. Of course, I am threatening checkmate in one move, but she can just play bishop to e2 and stop that. Except she can't because here I spotted one of the most beautiful sequences that I've ever played, starting with the move in question, the, in my opinion, brilliant bishop to e3, sacrificing a full bishop and attacking a bishop that is hanging. Of course, the black bishop can just be captured. What is the idea here? There is no back rank checkmate because both of these squares are defended by the bishop, but that is exactly where the problem lies. This one bishop is trying to defend two squares at the same time. So, rook to d1, another full piece sacrifice, and this time an entire rook. Rachel takes the rook, and now I play rook to f1. Of course, this is not a checkmate because the bishop can go back and defend the king. It seems like I lost two pieces for nothing. After rook takes d1, we are only down a rook and we have a passed pawn that is completely unstoppable. And these pieces are frozen. This one rook alone is keeping all of the white pieces at bay. If you move the knight, I'm going to win the rook. And if you create space for the rook to move like this, I'm going to win the knight. So, Rachel created space for the king to move, but I started to march with my pawn. The bishop is pinned to the king, so it cannot capture. The king comes out and I keep pushing. The bishop defends the promotion. And now a very important move, knight to e5. Not rushing with the promotion, we want to squeeze as much as possible from this position before promoting. Unfortunately, since this was a friendly over the board game, I don't have the ending of the game and I don't remember it. But from this position, I went on to confidently win. But here's the catch, the engine does not think that this is a brilliant move. What do you think?
